introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2022. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

Each question carries twenty-five marks. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Question 1(b) : l'ordre de grandeur « plus de 3000 mm à Douala » est un repère courant (Douala est l'une des villes les plus arrosées d'Afrique) ; à faire relire.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about » ou « more than ». Les faits cités sont à faire relire par un géographe avant toute mise en avant.

Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou`.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde puis page de questions), filigrane et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2022, THREE HOURS. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les figures déclarées sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) Distinguish between solar radiation and terrestrial radiation.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Solar radiation** (insolation) is the energy that reaches the Earth from the Sun. It is **short-wave radiation** (wavelengths of roughly 0.2 to 4 micrometres: ultraviolet, visible light and near infrared) because the Sun's surface is very hot (about 6000 K). **Terrestrial radiation** is the energy that the Earth's surface and atmosphere send back out. It is **long-wave (infrared) radiation** (wavelengths of roughly 4 to 100 micrometres, with a peak near 10 micrometres) because the Earth is much cooler (about 288 K on average).

| Point of difference | Solar radiation | Terrestrial radiation |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | The Sun | The Earth's surface (land, oceans) and the atmosphere |
| **Wavelength** | Short-wave, high energy | Long-wave (infrared), low energy |
| **Direction** | **Incoming** to the Earth | **Outgoing** from the Earth towards space |
| **When it operates** | In daytime only, and varies with latitude and season | Day and night, all the year |
| **Effect of the atmosphere** | The clear atmosphere is largely transparent to it, so much of it reaches the ground; about 30% is reflected or scattered back to space (the Earth's albedo) | The atmosphere is largely opaque to it: water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and other greenhouse gases absorb it and re-radiate part of it back to the ground |
| **Role in the heat budget** | The **input** that heats the Earth | The **output** that cools the Earth and balances the input |

**Conclusion.** Over the long term the incoming solar radiation is balanced by the outgoing terrestrial radiation plus the reflected part, which keeps the global mean temperature roughly stable. The greenhouse gases delay the escape of terrestrial radiation, and this natural **greenhouse effect** keeps the lower atmosphere about 33 °C warmer than it would otherwise be (about 15 °C on average instead of about -18 °C).

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) Examine **THREE** characteristics of Tropical Rainforest Climate.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **tropical rainforest (equatorial) climate** (Af in the Koppen system) is found within about 5 to 10 degrees of the Equator, for example the Congo Basin, southern Cameroon, the Amazon Basin and parts of South-East Asia. Three characteristics:

1. **Uniformly high temperatures all the year.** Mean monthly temperatures are about 25 to 28 °C, with a very small annual range (about 1 to 3 °C), because the Sun is high in the sky all the year and day length varies little. The diurnal (day-night) range, often 6 to 10 °C, is greater than the annual range.
2. **Heavy rainfall, well distributed through the year.** Annual totals are generally above about 2000 mm (more than 3000 mm at Douala on the Cameroon coast, which is exceptionally wet). There is no truly dry month, although southern Cameroon has two rainy seasons separated by a short, less rainy period. Much of the rain is **convectional**: intense afternoon thunderstorms caused by strong heating and the rise of moist air in the ITCZ (the zone of low pressure and converging air).
3. **High humidity and cloudiness.** Relative humidity is regularly above 80% because evaporation and evapotranspiration are intense; the sky is cloudy for much of the day and the air is sultry. Winds are light and variable (the doldrums).

Other acceptable points: low pressure (rising air), thick cloud and dew in the early morning, and the absence of a cold season.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Using any **TWO** of the following, explain the relationship between infiltration and overland flow.

(i) Rainfall intensity

(ii) Gradient

(iii) Soil characteristics.

(10 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Infiltration** is the downward entry of water from the surface into the soil. The **infiltration capacity** is the maximum rate at which a given soil can absorb water at a given time. **Overland flow** (surface runoff, Horton overland flow) is water that flows over the ground surface instead of entering the soil. The relationship is an **inverse** one: whatever rain cannot infiltrate becomes overland flow, so anything that raises infiltration lowers overland flow and anything that lowers infiltration increases it. The answer must deal with only TWO of the factors; rainfall intensity and soil characteristics are developed in full below, and gradient is given as a third option.

![fig-1](gce-al-geography-2022-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

**(i) Rainfall intensity**
- While the rainfall intensity (mm per hour) is **less** than the infiltration capacity, all the rain soaks in and there is no overland flow.
- When the intensity **exceeds** the capacity, the surplus first fills small hollows (depression storage), then flows over the surface. The excess is the overland flow (the shaded area on the diagram).
- The capacity itself **falls during a storm**, because the soil pores fill with water, clay particles swell and raindrop impact seals the surface. A long storm of only moderate intensity can therefore produce overland flow after a time (the "time of ponding").
- In the humid tropics, short and very intense convectional storms (which can reach several tens of millimetres per hour) readily exceed the capacity, which produces flash floods and gully erosion, especially on cleared land.

**(iii) Soil characteristics**
- **Texture and pore size**: sandy soils have large pores and a high capacity, so there is little overland flow; clay soils have tiny pores, take water slowly and generate much more runoff.
- **Structure and organic matter**: a crumb structure, roots, worm and termite channels and a humus-rich topsoil increase infiltration; a compacted, crusted or lateritic (ironpan) surface almost prevents it.
- **Soil moisture before the rain (antecedent moisture)**: dry soil absorbs rapidly, but a soil already saturated (after earlier rain or a high water table) has no free pore space, so even light rain runs off (saturation overland flow).
- **Depth** and the vegetation cover that protects the soil from raindrop impact also matter: bare, thin soils produce much more overland flow than forested soils.

**(ii) Gradient (alternative choice)**: on steep slopes water leaves quickly and has little time to soak in, so overland flow is high and infiltration low; on gentle slopes water is retained longer, ponds in hollows and infiltrates more. Steep slopes also have thin soils with less storage.

**Conclusion.** Overland flow rises when rainfall intensity is high, the slope steep and the soil clayey, compacted or already saturated. These factors determine the speed with which rivers respond to storms, and therefore the flood risk.
